entries.looks_like: The figures 925 struck in a small oblong punch, beside a maker's mark and, depending on the country, other marks.
entries.means: The metal is stated to be 925 parts silver in 1000: sterling. Struck by an assay office in the UK (where the number sits in a shield); stamped by the maker in the US and in Germany, where the law holds the maker to it.
entries.date_note: No single start date: each country's law sets when the number could be used (Germany from 1888; the UK number-in-shield mark is in british-hallmarks.json).

sources.where: Sched. 2: silver 925, standard mark the figures 925
(b)(1)–(2): fineness in parts per thousand; sterling at least 925/1000
§§ 2–3: fineness stated in thousandths, 800 or more
p. 19: the old standard of 11 oz 2 dwt in the pound troy (= 925/1000)

visual.object: Silver ware, Germany (date not given by the photographer)

entries.looks_like: The figures 800 struck in a small punch; in Germany from 1888 beside a crescent moon and a crown.
entries.means: The metal is stated to be 800 parts silver in 1000. It is the lowest UK standard for silver and the lowest fineness German law let a maker state on silver wares from 1888.
entries.date_note: Germany: stated fineness on silver wares only at 800 or more, from 1 January 1888.

sources.where: Sched. 2: silver 800, the figures 800
standards table: silver 800, 925, 958, 999
§ 2: silver fineness only 800 or more; § 10: in force 1 January 1888

visual.credit: Photograph: Phrontis, SilberPunze800.jpg, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0; cropped and toned by Heirloom.
visual.note: On this fork the crescent, crown and 800 share one punch outline; the crop takes only the 800 part. The maker's star is left out.

entries.looks_like: The figures 900 struck in a small punch.
entries.means: The metal is stated to be 900 parts silver in 1000, the US coin standard from 1837; in the US an item marked COIN must meet it.

sources.where: § 296: coin, 900/1000, four parts' tolerance
(b)(3): coin, at least 900/1000
introduction: 89.2% before 1837, 90% thereafter

searched: Wikimedia Commons: Category:Hallmarks and its country subcategories, Category:Nickel silver, Category:Silver plating hallmarks, and keyword searches (2026-11-22); searches for '900' silver marks returned only coins.
The Met Open Access: collection API returned 410 Gone and the website refused automated fetching (2026-11-22), so Met mark images could not be searched

Jewelers' Circular, Trade-Marks of the Jewelry and Kindred Trades (1896), archive.org: read all 220 pages' OCR and checked candidates on the page images: no 900 mark; the fineness numbers shown are 925 with STERLING.

Not reached: the 1904 and 1915 editions (not found on archive.org; HathiTrust not tried) and Rosenberg, Der Goldschmiede Merkzeichen (1911, 1922), which covers European goldsmiths' marks before about 1850 and isn't likely to show these American words.

Jewelers' Circular, Trade-Marks of the Jewelry and Kindred Trades (1922), HathiTrust hvd.hb9jsx, scans 146–220 (silverware and plated ware), read with on-device OCR and checked by eye: no 900 mark; the numbers shown are 925 and 925/1000 with STERLING.

entries.name: STERLING
entries.looks_like: The word STERLING (sometimes STER.) stamped in capitals, usually beside the maker's mark.
entries.means: The maker states the metal is at least 925 parts silver in 1000. Since 1906 US law forbids the word on anything below 925, and on plate.
entries.date_note: Sources differ on the start: French (1917) gives about 1857; Yale gives the change to sterling as by the 1860s.

sources.where: (b)(2) and note 1 (15 U.S.C. 297(a): not on plated wares)
glossary: 'About 1857 the word Sterling was stamped on silver articles'
introduction: sterling standard by the 1860s

searched: Wikimedia Commons: Category:Hallmarks and its country subcategories, Category:Nickel silver, Category:Silver plating hallmarks, and keyword searches (2026-11-22). Not checked: 'Arthur & Bond sterling silver wood tray mark.png' (CC BY-SA 4.0) is credited to The St. James's Collection, a dealer, which the database's rules exclude, so it was not considered.
Cooper Hewitt via Commons (CH files): American spoons and boxes found, front views only, no view of the mark
The Met Open Access: collection API returned 410 Gone and the website refused automated fetching (2026-11-22), so Met mark images could not be searched

Yale University Art Gallery pitcher retailed by Tiffany, marked ENGLISH STERLING 925-1000 (https://artgallery.yale.edu/collections/objects/64195): mark image and its licence not checked; Yale's open-access images are worth a second look.

Jewelers' Circular, Trade-Marks of the Jewelry and Kindred Trades (1896), archive.org: STERLING appears as typeset capitals under the trade-mark cuts or joined to a device (Lenau Co.'s L, p. 44; Meriden Britannia's phoenix, p. 45); none shows STERLING alone unambiguously.

1922 Jewelers' Circular (HathiTrust hvd.hb9jsx, scans 146–220; all 44 stand-alone STERLING hits checked by eye): only typeset, device-joined or one firm's script forms. Closest: Attleboro Mfg. Co.'s boxed STERLING (seq 150) shares its top edge with the triangles; Watrous Mfg. Co.'s STERLING (seq 180) is joined to an arrow; Frank Kursh & Son's script Sterling (p. 133, seq 162) is one firm's lettering, not the usual plain capitals.

entries.name: COIN
entries.looks_like: The word COIN in plain capitals, unframed, struck beside an early American maker's mark.
entries.means: The maker states the metal is of the standard of US silver coin: 892.4/1000 before 1837, 900/1000 after. Since 1906 US law requires 900 for the word.
entries.date_note: Mostly before the 1860s; French dates the word's use to after 1837.

sources.where: glossary: 'Coin — This word stamped by a die on silver after 1837 designated that the metal was of the same fineness as silver money'
objects stamped 'coin'
p. 28, 'Examples of maker's marks': COIN beside a maker's punch

visual.credit: Facsimile from The Jewelers' Circular, Trade-Marks of the Jewelry and Kindred Trades (1896), p. 28, public domain.
visual.note: The page shows COIN with the neighbouring maker's punch; the crop takes the word alone. The book doesn't name the maker. The word mark is about 33 px tall on the 2338 px page scan.

entries.name: PURE COIN
entries.looks_like: The words PURE COIN (or PURE SILVER COIN) stamped beside an American maker's mark.
entries.means: As COIN: the maker states the metal is of the US silver coin standard. Seen on New England silver.

entries.means: The maker states the metal is of the coin (dollar) standard. Found on silver made around Philadelphia.

entries.name: Crescent moon and crown
entries.looks_like: A crescent moon with a crown to its right, often in one shaped punch, struck beside the fineness number (800 or more) and the maker's mark.
entries.means: German silver ware of the stated fineness (at least 800), marked under the German Empire's law of 1884. The crescent stands for silver, the crown for the Reich. Not used on jewelry.
entries.date_note: From 1 January 1888; the end date isn't in these sources.

sources.where: the mark: Reichskrone, Mondsichel for silver, fineness in thousandths, the firm's mark; crown to the right of the crescent
marks: 'A crescent moon and crown are stamped beneath the base'

entries.name: NICKEL SILVER
entries.looks_like: The words NICKEL SILVER stamped in capitals, here over a second line, WEAR-WHITE, in the same punch.
entries.means: The item is nickel silver (German silver): an alloy of copper, nickel and zinc with no silver in it.
entries.date_note: The US Bureau of Standards noted in 1921 that the trade had moved from 'German silver' to 'nickel silver' after the war.

sources.where: whole entry

disagreements.note: Composition: Bureau of Standards, copper 52–80%, zinc 10–35%, nickel 5–30%; Meyers, brass with 16–33% nickel (usually 25%).

visual.credit: Photograph: Smirkybec, Nickel silver teaspoon marks.jpg, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0; cropped and toned by Heirloom.
visual.note: WEAR-WHITE is the second line of the same punch, read as a trade name; the number 12 and the maker's oval are left out.

entries.means: Alpacca (Alpaka): nickel silver, by the photographer's description; Meyers gives Alpaka as a name for silver-plated nickel silver. Either way the body has no silver.

entries.single_source: Only Meyers names Alpaka in a published source; that ALP marks nickel silver comes from the photographer's Commons description, not a published reference.

entries.name: GERMAN SILVER
entries.looks_like: The words GERMAN SILVER in hand-lettered capitals inside a rounded oblong outline, struck as its own punch.
entries.means: The item is German silver (nickel silver): copper, nickel and zinc, with no silver in it.
entries.date_note: Bureau of Standards (1921): the usual name until the trade moved to 'nickel silver' after the war.

entries.name: EPNS
entries.looks_like: The letters EPNS (sometimes E.P.N.S.) stamped in capitals, often with the maker's mark and a pattern or quality mark.
entries.means: Electroplated nickel silver: a nickel silver body with a thin coat of silver laid on by electroplating. The silver is only on the surface.
